value_chain_position: Factory and industrial automation equipment and software - programmable logic controllers, motor control centres and safety systems sold directly into factory and warehouse automation buildouts. Robotics and automation is the genuine primary chain; the grid, nuclear and power-for-artificial-intelligence overlaps are secondary end-market noise.
cost_curve_verified: Proxy versus company-reported: DISAGREE, materially. The bundle's deterministic metrics show revenue down 17.4% year on year on trailing-twelve-month sales of $6.66B, net debt at 2.19 times earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, and trailing free cash flow of $1.50B. All three are three-quarter artifacts - the data vendor's June-2026 income statement carries revenue as zero because Rockwell filed it the same morning (4 August 2026). Company-reported: third-quarter fiscal 2026 sales of $2.313B, up 8% as reported and 10% organically, with full-year guidance raised that morning to $8.968B-$9.134B; free cash flow of $654 million in the quarter alone, up 34%; and leverage of roughly 1.2 times on about $2.78B of net debt against roughly $2.33B of full-year earnings before those items. There is no output commodity and therefore no unit cost curve; the equivalent load-bearing figure is the operating margin, which is verified below.
gm_trajectory: Expanding, but the proxy measures the wrong thing. The bundle's +8.2 point three-year gross-margin expansion to 48.1% is almost entirely a reporting reclassification: research and development, about 7.8% of sales, sat inside cost of revenue through fiscal 2025 and is broken out separately from fiscal 2026. On a like-for-like basis gross margin is roughly 41.7% in the June 2026 quarter against 40.9% a year earlier, up about 0.8 points on 10% organic growth. The genuine pricing-power evidence is the company's own operating-margin disclosure of 4 August 2026: enterprise operating margin 22.3% versus 19.5% a year ago, with all three segments expanding simultaneously (Software and Control 34.8% versus 31.6%, Intelligent Devices 20.0% versus 18.8%, Lifecycle Services 15.1% versus 13.3%). Expanding margin on growing revenue is real pricing power here - but note management's own repeated caveat that a meaningful slice of the reported 2%-plus price realisation is tariff pass-through, deliberately run neutral to earnings.
bull_thesis:
Rockwell is the installed base of American factory automation, and it has just finished converting a two-year downturn into a structurally better business. The evidence is in the company's own audited figures rather than in management's adjectives. In the quarter ended June 2026, reported on 4 August, sales grew 10% organically to $2.313 billion, enterprise operating profit rose 23% to $516 million, and margin reached 22.3% against 19.5% a year earlier - with every segment expanding at once. Free cash flow was $654 million in the quarter, up 34%. Management raised full-year adjusted earnings guidance to $13.00-$13.30 per share, the fourth raise in twelve months, and lifted organic growth guidance to 7.5%-9.5% from 5%-9%.

The mix change underneath is the real bull case. Software and Control - the Logix control platform plus the FactoryTalk and Plex software portfolio - grew 19% to $751 million at a 34.8% operating margin, above the company's own stated 31%-to-34% medium-term corridor. That segment is now roughly half of the group's operating profit on under a third of its revenue. Switching costs there are genuine: replacing a Logix controller means re-engineering and re-validating a production line, which is why the chief executive could say in February 2026 that the company's artificial-intelligence tools 'fortify and complement the existing system' rather than requiring a rip-out. On his August 2025 account, Logix unit shipments are still below pre-2020 levels, so the margin gains are not a volume-peak artifact - there is recovery still to come in the highest-margin product line.

Demand is broad and, unusually for this lane, named and shipping rather than promised. Autonomous mobile robots are in production at Subaru of Indiana; control systems are going into a new artificial-intelligence data centre in Texas with ATS Automation; GSK has standardised on the Verve cybersecurity platform across 33 sites over five years; Stanley Electric is deploying Plex across 25 sites; Hyundai in Georgia, Lucid in Saudi Arabia, Thermo Fisher, Freshpet, Hindalco and Butantan are all named production deployments across the last five calls. There is no material single-customer concentration because Rockwell sells largely through distribution. Data-centre sales more than doubled year on year in the March 2026 quarter, e-commerce and warehouse automation grew over 30%, and semiconductor grew high teens.

Capital discipline through the last cycle was sound: capital expenditure has run under 2% of sales, the balance sheet carries about 1.2 times leverage with an Altman-Z solvency score of 6.1 and a Piotroski quality score of 8 out of 9, and management dissolved its failed Sensia joint venture with SLB in November 2025 with an explicit public admission that it 'did not meet our long-term expectations' - taking back the profitable process-automation piece and lifting the Lifecycle Services margin in the process. The $2 billion five-year investment programme announced in August 2025 is mostly growth capital expenditure but is explicitly designed to keep the number of rooftops flat, so it is a productivity build, not a capacity land-grab.

Conditions the bull case depends on: the North American manufacturing capital-expenditure cycle continuing to broaden, the data-centre and warehouse-automation engines proving to be multi-year build-outs rather than a two-year pull-forward, incremental margins holding above the 35% management signed up for, and Software and Control sustaining margins near the top of its corridor. If those hold and fiscal 2027 earnings reach roughly $14.60-$15.00 per share, a peer-parity multiple gets you to the low $500s.
bear_thesis:
The business is excellent and the price already says so. Rockwell trades at 33.8 times its own fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings guidance of $13.15 per share and roughly 26 times enterprise value to operating profit, against Emerson at about 19 times enterprise value to earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, Siemens at about 16 times and ABB at about 24 times. Every valuation model in the screener stack - discounted cash flow, earnings power value, Graham, owner earnings - returns a margin of safety of minus 100%. The consensus analyst target of $484 sits about 9% above the current price, and the lowest published target, $430, is below it.

The critical fact is what the earnings recovery actually represents. Fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings of about $13.15 per share are only around 8% above the fiscal 2023 peak of roughly $12.12, reached three years earlier. Over that span the shares re-rated from about 20 times forward earnings to about 34. The earnings recovered; the multiple did the work. That is a peak-multiple-on-recovered-earnings setup, and it is exactly the configuration that punishes hardest when the cycle turns.

The adverse path is specific and priceable. First, the growth engines are the most capital-expenditure-sensitive end markets Rockwell serves - data centres, e-commerce and warehouse automation, semiconductors - and management has never sized any of them, while describing the company as 'largely a flow company' with new-capacity projects only 'a little bit more than it would have been in the past.' A hyperscaler digestion pause removes the entire growth differential. Second, commodities are an input cost here, not a revenue tailwind: management flagged a double-digit-million-dollar memory-chip inflation headwind for the second half of fiscal 2026 on the May 2026 call, and has stated repeatedly that tariff-based pricing is run neutral to earnings by design - so it cannot be used to offset input cost inflation. Rising copper, memory and fuel compress this business; they do not lift it. Third, the productivity lever is spent: the $325 million of fiscal-2025 structural savings is, in the chief financial officer's own November 2025 words, 'built into our base.' Fourth, the current margin is flagged as unsustainable by the company itself - Software and Control at 34.8% is above its own 31%-to-34% corridor, and management said second-half spending returns.

The near-term arithmetic already shows the deceleration. The raised full-year guidance implies a fourth quarter of about $2.39 billion in sales, up roughly 3% year on year against the 8% just delivered, and about $3.61 in adjusted earnings per share, up roughly 8% against the 22% just delivered. That is management guiding its own final quarter to a sharp slowdown, and it is why the shares fell 7.55% on a beat-and-raise.

What would confirm the bear case: the Lifecycle Services book-to-bill ratio falling below 1.0 for two consecutive quarters outside the normal fourth-quarter seasonality (it has run 1.07, 1.06, 0.90, 1.16, 1.07 across the last five calls); the return of a total-company book-to-bill disclosure, which management removed from the regular cadence in May 2025 and now publishes only when the ratio is outside its normal range - so its reappearance is itself a signal; Software and Control margin falling back into the low 30s; or fiscal 2027 guidance in November implying incremental margins below 35%. Two governance details corroborate the caution: the company repurchased 0.3 million shares for $145 million during the June 2026 quarter at roughly $483 each, within a few percent of the all-time high and above today's price; and insiders have made zero open-market purchases against 49 sales totalling 55,404 shares.

In a genuine down-cycle - Rockwell's own fiscal 2024 saw revenue fall 9% - sales of roughly $8.3 billion at an 18% enterprise margin produce about $9.90 per share of earnings power. On a trough multiple of about 20 times, that is roughly $200 per share. The downside is not a solvency event; it is a 50%-plus de-rating of a perfectly healthy company.
sop_bull: $510 per share. Parts valued on enterprise value to segment operating profit at full peer parity, using fiscal 2027 earning power (operating profit up about 10% on continued 7%-9% organic growth). Software and Control: about $3.2 billion of revenue at a 34%-35% margin, roughly $1.13 billion of operating profit at 28 times = $31.6 billion - a premium to the peer group justified by the Logix installed-base switching costs, 19% growth and a margin two-thirds higher than the group average. Intelligent Devices: about $4.6 billion of revenue at 20%-21%, roughly $940 million of operating profit at 23 times = $21.6 billion, in line with ABB and Emerson, which trade near 27 times enterprise value to operating profit. Lifecycle Services: about $2.0 billion of revenue at 15%-16% post-Sensia, roughly $310 million at 14 times = $4.3 billion. Corporate costs of about $160 million at 23 times = minus $3.7 billion. Enterprise value $53.8 billion, less net debt of about $2.6 billion after another year of cash generation, gives equity of $51.2 billion. Cross-check: this is roughly 35 times fiscal 2027 earnings of about $14.60 per share - the current premium multiple sustained on grown earnings, and consistent with the highest published street target of $525. On 111.5 million diluted shares: about $510 per share.
sop_bear: $195 per share, assuming the chain regime turns against it - North American manufacturing capital expenditure rolls over, the data-centre and warehouse-automation order surge normalises, automotive and consumer-packaged-goods deferrals persist, and memory, copper and fuel inflation compresses a margin that has just peaked. Software and Control: revenue down 10% to about $2.66 billion at a 31% margin (the bottom of management's own stated corridor), $824 million of operating profit at 20 times = $16.5 billion. Intelligent Devices: revenue down 12% to about $3.74 billion at a 16% margin (the fiscal 2024-2025 level), $598 million at 14 times = $8.4 billion. Lifecycle Services: revenue down 8% to about $1.75 billion at 12%, $210 million at 9 times = $1.9 billion. Corporate costs of $150 million at 16 times = minus $2.4 billion. Enterprise value $24.4 billion, less net debt of about $3.0 billion (leverage rises as the dividend and buyback continue into a weaker cash year), gives equity of $21.4 billion, or about $192 per share on 111.5 million diluted shares. A top-down cross-check - revenue of $8.3 billion at an 18% enterprise margin, $1.49 billion of operating profit at 18 times, less net debt - lands at about $214. The parts and the top-down bracket $190-$215. Note this is a de-rating, not a distress case: net debt at roughly 1.2 times earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation and an Altman-Z solvency score of 6.1 leave no financing risk at all.
sop_breakdown: Base case, fiscal 2026 run-rate segment operating profit valued on enterprise value to operating profit, anchored to the true competitor set. Software and Control: about $2.95 billion of revenue at a 34.8% margin, $1,027 million of operating profit at 28 times = $28.8 billion. This carries the premium multiple because it holds the switching-cost moat and grew 19%, but it is discounted from a pure-software rating because roughly two-thirds of the segment's revenue is Logix hardware, not software. Intelligent Devices: about $4.25 billion of revenue at a 20.0% margin, $850 million at 21 times = $17.9 billion, a modest discount to ABB and Emerson at roughly 27 times enterprise value to operating profit, on the grounds that this is the more hardware-cyclical, more North-America-exposed half of the company and has just printed a peak margin. Lifecycle Services: about $1.90 billion of revenue at a 15.1% margin, $287 million at 12 times = $3.4 billion, reflecting project-services economics and a base still shrinking on the Sensia dissolution. Corporate costs of about $150 million a year at 21 times = minus $3.2 billion. Enterprise value $46.9 billion, less net debt of $2.78 billion (borrowings of $3.26 billion less $479 million of cash at 30 June 2026, on the ex-lease definition the filings usually quote - this is a liability and is subtracted), gives equity of $44.1 billion. On 111.5 million diluted shares: $395. The blended implied multiple is about 23 times enterprise value to operating profit - a clear premium to Siemens at roughly 21 times, a discount to ABB and Emerson at roughly 27. Independent cross-check on earnings: $395 is about 27 times estimated fiscal 2027 earnings of $14.60 per share, generous against a ten-year history nearer 22-24 times, and the two methods agree in a $365-$410 band.
risk_reward: Unattractive at $444.65. The base-case sum-of-the-parts fair value of $395 sits about 11% BELOW the current price - you are paying above intrinsic value, not below it. Upside to the favourable case is $510; the adverse case is $205. So the levels are: downside-to-break $205, base $395, upside $510 against a live price of $444.65. There is no structural floor - no deal terms, no net cash, no tender; the company carries $2.78 billion of net debt, so the only support under the shares is the multiple investors are willing to pay, which is precisely the variable at risk. The asymmetry runs the wrong way at this price: roughly two and a half times more room to the adverse case than to the favourable one.
catalyst_status_note: The load-bearing event fired this morning. Rockwell reported third-quarter fiscal 2026 results before the open on 4 August 2026 (Business Wire release, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission at 07:01 Eastern): sales of $2.313 billion up 8% reported and 10% organic, adjusted earnings of $3.49 per share against a $3.38-$3.39 consensus, diluted earnings of $3.65 up 40%, enterprise operating margin of 22.3% versus 19.5%, free cash flow of $654 million up 34%, and full-year guidance raised to $13.00-$13.30 adjusted earnings per share and 7.5%-9.5% organic growth from $12.50-$13.10 and 5%-9%. The shares fell 7.55% to $444.65 on the print. The re-rate on this event is not merely spent - it went the other way. Under this lane's rules that is descriptive only and carries no penalty: the value question is judged on the residual gap to fair value, which is what drives the call below.
peer_comps_note: Assigned true competitors, priced on trailing twelve months as of 4 August 2026: Emerson at 35.5 times earnings and 19.2 times enterprise value to earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (about 27 times enterprise value to operating profit); ABB at 36.4 times earnings and 24.4 times those earnings (about 27 times operating profit); Siemens at 28.9 times earnings and 16.3 times (about 21 times operating profit). Honeywell screens at 9.2 times earnings and 7.9 times, but that is distorted by separation accounting and is not a usable comparison. Rockwell at $444.65 trades at 33.8 times its own fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings guidance and about 26 times enterprise value to operating profit - level with ABB and Emerson, at a clear premium to Siemens. Rockwell earns some of that premium: the highest operating margin in the group at 22.3%, the highest return on equity at 36.2%, and the purest automation exposure. What it does not support is a further re-rating. There is no relative-value discount to harvest here; the sum-of-the-parts fair value of $395 corresponds to about 23 times operating profit, between Siemens and the ABB/Emerson pair, which is where a business of this quality and this cyclicality belongs.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is not about the business - it is about what the last twelve months proved. The street has published six price targets in the last quarter averaging $493.50, against twenty over the past year averaging $437.60, with the newest at $500 (Chris Dankert, 15 June 2026), $501 (Bernstein, 9 June 2026), $525 (Christopher Snyder, 6 May 2026) and $510 (KeyBanc, 6 May 2026). Those targets embed three assumptions we think are wrong.

First, that incremental margins above 50% are a run-rate. They are not. Management originally signed up for 35% incrementals at two consecutive investor days, then guided to 40%, and the above-50% outcome in fiscal 2026 is the harvest of a specific, finite programme - $325 million of structural productivity in fiscal 2025 against a $250 million target - plus the optical lift from deconsolidating the Sensia joint venture on 1 April 2026. The chief financial officer said in November 2025 that those savings are now 'built into our base.' You cannot cut the same cost twice. Fiscal 2027 has to be carried by volume and genuine price, and management has told you the tariff component of price is run neutral to earnings by design.

Second, that the fastest-growing end markets are an annuity. Data-centre sales more than doubled year on year in the March 2026 quarter, e-commerce and warehouse automation grew over 30%, semiconductor grew high teens. Rockwell has never sized any of them, and the chief executive has said the company remains 'largely a flow company' with new-capacity projects only 'a little bit more than it would have been in the past.' The street is capitalising a capital-expenditure surge in an undisclosed slice of revenue at an annuity multiple.

Third, and most important, that $13.15 of adjusted earnings represents a new plateau. It is only about 8% above the fiscal 2023 peak of roughly $12.12, three years later. Across that period the multiple went from about 20 times forward earnings to about 34. The street has extrapolated an earnings recovery into a permanent re-rating. We think the earnings are real and the re-rating is borrowed.

One place the market is closer to right than the screener: the deterministic metrics in our own bundle read revenue down 17.4% and leverage at 2.19 times. Both are three-quarter data artifacts. Anyone shorting this on the screener's revenue line would be shorting a data-vendor bug.
valley_of_death:
The risky window is the next three to nine months, and it is a multiple problem rather than a balance-sheet problem. There is no cash-burn hump and no maturity wall: net debt of about $2.78 billion sits at roughly 1.2 times fiscal 2026 earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, interest expense runs about $33 million a quarter against $516 million of quarterly operating profit, the Altman-Z solvency score is 6.1 and the Piotroski quality score is 8 out of 9. Free cash flow was $654 million in the June quarter alone.

What can go wrong is earnings momentum, and management has already guided to it. The raised full-year outlook implies a September-quarter result of roughly $2.39 billion in sales, up about 3% year on year against the 8% just delivered, and roughly $3.61 in adjusted earnings per share, up about 8% against the 22% just delivered. Four specific pressures sit inside that quarter. Memory-chip inflation, which the chief financial officer described on the May 2026 call as 'real' and worth a double-digit-million-dollar headwind in the second half. Engineering, development and project spending that he said explicitly 'comes back in the second half.' The Sensia dissolution subtracting roughly $50 million of revenue a quarter. And a Software and Control margin of 34.8% that is above the company's own 31%-to-34% corridor and which management has flagged will come down.

Then comes the harder gate: fiscal 2027 guidance at the fourth-quarter print in early November 2026, against a comparison base that includes above-50% incremental margins and 7.5%-9.5% organic growth. A first guide in the 5%-7% organic range with incrementals back at 35% would be an entirely normal outcome and would still look like a downgrade against a 34-times multiple.

The compounding risk is that the order book is now partly invisible. Management removed the total-company book-to-bill ratio from its regular disclosure in May 2025, publishing it only when it falls outside the normal range. The one series still published each quarter, Lifecycle Services, has run 1.07, 1.06, 0.90, 1.16 and 1.07 across the last five calls - healthy - but it covers roughly a fifth of revenue. If demand rolls over in the product businesses, the first hard evidence arrives in the sales line, not ahead of it.
positioning_washout:
There is no mechanical, forced-selling dynamic here, and it would be dishonest to manufacture one. Rockwell pays a modest dividend of about 1.2%, has a long record of increases, is not cutting it, and is not pivoting its business model - so the dividend-focused and index shareholder base has no trigger to liquidate. Leverage is low enough that no covenant or ratings action is in prospect.

The selling pressure that does exist is discretionary and momentum-driven, and it started today. The shares had risen roughly 45% off a 52-week low of $305.44 to a high of $497.36, sat 17% above the 200-day moving average and near the top of the 52-week range going into the print, and then fell 7.55% on a beat with raised guidance. That combination - good news, sharply lower price - is the signature of crowded positioning unwinding rather than a fundamental break. Growth and momentum money that bought the recovery has an exit to make, and the smart-money and institutional-flow readings in our bundle (73 and 50 out of 100) suggest ownership is broad rather than concentrated in conviction hands.

Insider behaviour points the same way: zero open-market purchases against 49 sales totalling 55,404 shares. And the company itself bought 0.3 million shares for $145 million during the June quarter at roughly $483 each - above today's price. When the buyer of last resort has been paying more than the current market, there is no repurchase bid waiting underneath.

The practical read: expect the de-rating to be orderly and multi-week rather than a single violent flush. That matters for the entry plan below, because a name with no forced seller rarely gives you a capitulation print.
forcing_function:
Three dates, of descending usefulness. The first has already passed: the third-quarter fiscal 2026 release on 4 August 2026, which delivered the beat, the guidance raise and a 7.55% fall. That was the re-rating event, and it re-rated downward.

The next hard date is the fourth-quarter and full-year fiscal 2026 report in early November 2026, which carries first guidance for fiscal 2027 - the number that decides whether above-50% incremental margins were a programme or a plateau. Alongside it, management promised at the August 2025 call to detail the scope and milestones of the $2 billion five-year investment programme, and it has an investor day cadence in November. That is the single event most likely to reset the multiple in either direction.

The third is a disclosure event rather than a calendar one, and it is the most information-dense signal available: management publishes the total-company book-to-bill ratio only when it sits outside its normal range. Its reappearance in any release is therefore itself the news, in whichever direction it points.

But the honest answer for this name is that the forcing function we need is a price event, not a company event. The business does not need a catalyst to be worth owning; it needs to trade closer to what it is worth. The specific trigger for us is a retest of the $360-$380 zone - roughly 25 to 26 times estimated fiscal 2027 earnings of about $14.60 per share, and a 4%-9% discount to our $395 base-case value. Equivalently, a fiscal 2027 organic growth guide of 5% or better in November combined with a share price under $400 would open the position on fundamentals rather than on a flush.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a genuinely excellent operator at a demanding price, and the discipline required is to keep those two facts apart.

The operating position is verified and strong. Third-quarter fiscal 2026 results published on 4 August 2026 show sales of $2.313 billion up 10% organically, enterprise operating margin of 22.3% against 19.5% a year earlier, margin expansion in all three segments simultaneously, free cash flow of $654 million up 34%, and full-year guidance raised for the fourth time in twelve months to $13.00-$13.30 of adjusted earnings per share. The pricing-power test this lane cares about - expanding margin on growing revenue - passes on the company's own audited operating-margin disclosure, though not for the reason the screener thinks: the deterministic gross-margin signal is an accounting-reclassification artifact, and the real like-for-like gross-margin gain is about 0.8 points, with the rest coming from operating leverage and a finite productivity programme.

The order book is the weakest link in an otherwise clean file, and it is weak by choice: management withdrew the total-company book-to-bill ratio from regular disclosure in May 2025. What remains is good - the Lifecycle Services ratio at 1.07 and a dense list of named, dated production deployments rather than memoranda of understanding, from Subaru of Indiana to GSK's 33-site cybersecurity standardisation to control systems in a Texas artificial-intelligence data centre. Capital discipline through the last cycle was sound, with capital expenditure under 2% of sales and a failed joint venture killed in public in November 2025. The one blemish is repurchasing $145 million of stock at roughly $483 a share during the June quarter, within a few percent of the all-time high.

On the chain: automation demand reads neutral rather than favourable, and commodities are input costs here, not revenue. Rising memory, copper and fuel prices compress this business - management has flagged a double-digit-million-dollar memory headwind for the second half and has committed to running tariff-driven pricing neutral to earnings, which removes the obvious offset.

Which brings it to price. At $444.65 the shares carry 33.8 times fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings and about 26 times enterprise value to operating profit - level with ABB and Emerson, at a premium to Siemens. The sum-of-the-parts, built segment by segment on those same peer multiples, lands at $395, about 11% below the market. The decisive fact is that fiscal 2026's record adjusted earnings of roughly $13.15 sit only about 8% above the fiscal 2023 peak reached three years earlier, while the multiple went from about 20 times to about 34. The earnings recovered; the re-rating did the rest of the work, and it is that borrowed portion at risk. In a normal down-cycle - Rockwell's own fiscal 2024 saw revenue fall 9% - the parts point to roughly $195 a share, a de-rating rather than a distress event.

So the call is to wait for the wash-out, not to pass and not to buy. Passing outright would be wrong: this is a wide and widening moat, built on the switching costs of the Logix installed base, with credible management, a four-raise track record, immaculate solvency and Logix unit volumes still below pre-2020 levels. Buying here would be worse: you would be paying 11% above intrinsic value, with the company's own guidance implying its September quarter decelerates from 22% earnings growth to about 8%, and with no floor underneath the shares other than the multiple itself. The level to wait for is $360-$380 - roughly 25 to 26 times estimated fiscal 2027 earnings, and a real discount to fair value. Given that there is no forced seller in this shareholder base, expect that de-rating to arrive slowly if it arrives at all. That is an acceptable cost of patience for a business this good.

Separately on the pure value question, ignoring any event overlay: the forensic file is clean and the franchise durable, but the price is above our reconciled fair value and every valuation model in the stack returns no margin of safety. Quality does not make an expensive stock cheap.
